Getting started with manifest

Source: vignettes/manifest.Rmd
manifest.Rmd

Why keep a manifest?

Before a dataset reaches a model it is usually sampled: outliers are trimmed, a geography or time window is chosen, invalid records are removed. Each of these decisions changes who is in the analysis and who is not, yet the reasoning behind them tends to live only in the analyst’s head or in scattered code comments. Months later — during peer review, replication, or a hand-off — it can be surprisingly hard to answer a simple question: how did we get from the raw data to the modeling sample, and why?

The manifest package produces a lightweight audit trail for exactly this stage of the workflow. You bracket your filtering code with begin_manifest() and end_manifest(), and the package records, for every row-reducing step:

  • a human-readable rationale (drawn from #: comments in the code),
  • the exact code that ran,
  • the number and percentage of rows dropped, and
  • the rows remaining.

The result is printed as a table and saved as a timestamped CSV that can travel with your project as documentation of the sampling framework.

Comment conventions

manifest reads your script and treats comments differently depending on their prefix:

Prefix Meaning Captured in the manifest?
#: Manifest criteria Yes — becomes the CRITERIA text
#: {name} ... Step label Yes — becomes the STEP label
## Dev / internal note No
# Ordinary comment No

A #: comment sitting directly above a filtering call is paired with that call. This lets you write the reason for a decision as a normal comment and have it promoted automatically into the documentation.

A worked example

The package ships a complete, runnable example. Here is the script in full — note the #: {name} labels and #: rationales above each filtering step:

# example_cleaning.R
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A self-contained example of the manifest workflow. Run it with:
#
#   script <- system.file("examples", "example_cleaning.R", package = "manifest")
#   source(script)
#
# Because it is run via source(), begin_manifest() auto-detects this file's
# path and end_manifest() can back-fill the CRITERIA / CODE columns from the
# `#:` comments below. The timestamped CSV is written under tempdir().
#
# Comment key:
#   #:   Manifest criteria  - appears in the CRITERIA column of the manifest
#   ##   Dev / internal note - ignored by manifest
#   #    Ordinary comment    - ignored by manifest
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(dplyr)
library(manifest)

## -- Simulate a raw dataset ---------------------------------------------------
set.seed(42)
d <- data.frame(
  id    = 1:1000,
  x     = rnorm(1000, mean = 8, sd = 3),
  state = sample(c("MN", "SD", "ND", "WI", "IA"), 1000, replace = TRUE),
  year  = sample(2018:2023, 1000, replace = TRUE),
  score = rnorm(1000, 50, 15)
)

## -- Open the manifest --------------------------------------------------------
begin_manifest(
  data         = d,
  description  = "Simulated dataset created to demonstrate package functionality",
  build_script = "compile_data.R",
  output_dir   = file.path(tempdir(), "manifest"),
  dataset_name = "package_demo_data",
  verbose      = TRUE
)

## QA note: x values were validated against source registry on 2024-01-15
#: {name} Drop outliers in X
#: Omit records where X statistic exceeds 10 (outliers per pre-reg criteria)
d <- mfilter(d, x <= 10)

## We originally considered all 5 states; ND/WI/IA dropped for sample size
#: {name} Study geography
#: Restrict study to Minnesota and South Dakota (primary catchment states)
d <- mfilter(d, state %in% c("MN", "SD"))

#: {name} Study time period
#: Limit to study period 2020-2022
d <- mfilter(d, year >= 2020, year <= 2022)

## Score < 0 is a data entry artifact; confirmed with PI on 2024-02-03
#: Remove records with invalid scores (score < 0 indicates data entry error)
d <- mfilter(d, score >= 0)

## -- Close the manifest, write the CSV, print the summary ---------------------
end_manifest(d)

Because the example is executed with source(), begin_manifest() auto-detects the script’s path, so end_manifest() can read it back and back-fill the CRITERIA and CODE columns from the #: comments. Run it:

library(manifest)

script <- system.file("examples", "example_cleaning.R", package = "manifest")
source(script)

end_manifest() also wrote a timestamped CSV. Reading it back shows the structured record that would live alongside your project:

out_dir  <- file.path(tempdir(), "manifest")
csv_file <- tail(sort(list.files(out_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)), 1)

knitr::kable(read.csv(csv_file, check.names = FALSE))
STEP DROPPED DROPPED_PCT REMAIN REMAIN_PCT CRITERIA CODE
START NA 1000 100% description{Simulated dataset created to demonstrate package functionality} source{compile_data.R}
(1) Drop outliers in X 248 24.8% 752 75.2% Omit records where X statistic exceeds 10 (outliers per pre-reg criteria) d <- mfilter(d, x <= 10)
(2) Study geography 471 47.1% 281 28.1% Restrict study to Minnesota and South Dakota (primary catchment states) d <- mfilter(d, state %in% c(“MN”, “SD”))
(3) Study time period 134 13.4% 147 14.7% Limit to study period 2020-2022 d <- mfilter(d, year >= 2020, year <= 2022)
(4) 0 0.0% 147 14.7% Remove records with invalid scores (score < 0 indicates data entry error) d <- mfilter(d, score >= 0)

Anatomy of the workflow

begin_manifest(data, ...) opens the log and records the starting row count. Two arguments are worth calling out:

  • description — a sentence about the dataset, stored on the START row.
  • build_script — the path to the script that assembled the raw data (often distinct from the cleaning script you are annotating). It is recorded so the manifest points back to the data’s origin.

mfilter(data, ...) is a drop-in replacement for dplyr::filter(). It applies the filter and records the row delta. Pair it with a #: comment on the line above to supply the rationale automatically.

end_manifest(data) parses the script for #: comments, back-fills the CRITERIA / CODE columns, prints the summary table, and writes the CSV.

manifest_log() lets you peek at the running log at any point before end_manifest().

Reading the columns

Column Meaning
STEP Step number, plus the name label if one was given
DROPPED Rows removed by this step
DROPPED_PCT Those rows as a share of the starting N
REMAIN Rows still in play after the step
REMAIN_PCT Remaining rows as a share of the starting N
CRITERIA The rationale, from the #: comment
CODE The exact expression that ran

Note that percentages are always relative to the original row count, so REMAIN_PCT reads as “share of the raw data still in the modeling sample” — a convenient headline number for a methods section.

Steps that aren’t simple filters

Not every row-reducing operation is a filter(). Joins, de-duplication, and aggregation also drop rows, and for those you can log the step manually with log_step(), passing the rationale explicitly via criteria =:

library(dplyr)

set.seed(1)
roster <- data.frame(
  id     = 1:20,
  region = sample(c("A", "B"), 20, replace = TRUE),
  active = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 20, replace = TRUE)
)

begin_manifest(
  roster,
  description  = "Toy roster to demonstrate log_step()",
  output_dir   = file.path(tempdir(), "roster-manifest"),
  dataset_name = "roster",
  verbose      = FALSE
)

# A normal filter, tracked automatically:
roster <- mfilter(roster, active)

# A de-duplication that filter() can't express — log it by hand:
roster <- roster[!duplicated(roster$region), ]
roster <- log_step(roster, criteria = "Keep one representative record per region")

manifest_log()
#>   STEP DROPPED DROPPED_PCT REMAIN REMAIN_PCT
#>  START      NA                 20       100%
#>    (1)       8       40.0%     12      60.0%
#>    (2)      10       50.0%      2      10.0%
#>                                           CRITERIA CODE
#>  description{Toy roster to demonstrate log_step()}     
#>                                                        
#>          Keep one representative record per region

Here mfilter() and log_step() interleave freely, and log_step() carries its own criteria string rather than relying on a #: comment. Call end_manifest() when you are done to finalize the table and write the CSV, just as in the first example.
